# Discussion {#sec-discussion .deo-discussion}

This review asked what citizen involvement looks like at each stage of research,
and which initiatives, in Indonesia and elsewhere, have put it into practice.
Across eight cases, citizens held leading roles at every stage only where the
group that founded the initiative led the work: the Patient-Led Research
Collaborative and LaporCovid-19. In those two cases, involvement changed the
research question and produced evidence before official or conventional sources
did. In the other six cases, citizen roles were mostly limited to data
collection and to consultation on selected components, and in the two failures
the people whose data were used had no research role at all. No item was met in
six or more of the eight cases, and twelve of the eighteen items were met in two
or fewer. The most consistently lacking practices were returning results to
participants, letting contributors choose their credit, evaluating the project,
opening data and results, and documenting consent and ethics review, and for
most of these the sources simply did not say. These findings are consistent with
the systematic review of citizen science in mental health, which found that
citizen scientists contributed mostly through data collection and that
feedback, data availability and attribution were rarely reported
[@todowede2023].

Citizen leadership and uptake did not go together. The two founder-led cases
changed which questions were asked, but documented use of their findings by
decision-makers was partial: LaporCovid-19's data challenged official figures
and its relationship with government stayed contested [@laporcovid2021], and
findings from the Patient-Led Research Collaborative drew attention without a
documented route into decisions in the sources we reviewed. The only case with
documented uptake, the Indonesian Red Cross community-based surveillance, was
designed with government stakeholders and built into the national early-warning
system and local budgets, but its volunteers reported to a protocol designed by
others and had no role in analysis [@ifrc2021]. Both failures began with an
organisation acting on behalf of people in distress without asking them. With
one clear success among eight purposively chosen cases, we cannot say what
produces uptake. The pattern does raise a practical question: how can citizen
leadership over the question be combined with the institutional routes through
which findings become policy or programmes? The next sections set out three
conditions that the cases point to, and then apply them to Indonesia. They are
recommendations for future practice, not tested findings.

The first condition is a pathway from findings to decisions, agreed at the design
stage with a named institutional counterpart. In the Red Cross case the
counterpart was part of the design: alerts fed into the national early-warning
system, and local governments took ownership, with Boyolali prioritising the
programme in its budget [@ifrc2021]. CoAct shows the weaker version. Its
assembly produced 14 recommendations and public commitments from a city
councillor and the director of the National Mental Health Pact, yet we could
trace no adoption [@ub2022assembly; @bcn2023plan], which suggests that
commitments need to be recorded and followed up. Youth-GEMS states openly where
young people's involvement stops and why [@youthgems_decisions2025], a clear
role agreement that institutions can accept. In LaporCovid-19, the health-worker
database was built with professional associations, a news organisation and a
research unit, and the analysis had Ministry of Health ethics approval
[@ekawati2022]. This is a single observation, but it shows that a civil-society
database can gain institutional standing without being run by an institution.
Wider evidence points the same way, with caution. A systematic review of 145
studies found that collaboration and relationships between researchers and
policymakers were among the most often reported facilitators of evidence use,
and that poor access to relevant research and research arriving too late were
the main barriers [@oliver2014]. A scoping review of integrated knowledge
translation, in which research is done in partnership with decision-makers from
the outset, found that most evaluated partnerships reported at least one
positive outcome, but it is not known which partnership strategies lead to which
outcomes [@gagliardi2016]. In Indonesia, a ministerial regulation already
defines community-based surveillance and how volunteers are recruited and
organised at village level, but it covers zoonoses and emerging infectious
diseases only [@permenkopmk7_2022]. We cite it as an analogy for what a pathway
could look like, not as a legal basis for mental-health reporting.

A benchmark outside our eight cases is the NIH RECOVER programme on Long COVID.
The protocol of its adult cohort states that patient representatives give input
on all study processes, and some were recruited from advocacy groups including
the Patient-Led Research Collaborative [@horwitz2023]; representatives have
described the partnership from their side [@kim2023]. Embedding patients in a
research programme is not the same as institutions using findings that patients
generated (item C3), and the depth of embedding is open to question. A survey of
members of RECOVER's clinical-trial protocol working groups found that most
patient, caregiver and community representatives felt their input was valued,
but gaps in role clarity, communication and integration of feedback persisted
[@leverty2026]. We found no peer-reviewed account of the policy influence of the
Collaborative's survey. A news feature in *Nature*, which is journalism and not
peer-reviewed evidence, reported that the survey had been mentioned in some 60
policy statements and that patient-led efforts had helped to shape research
programmes [@fairbank2024]. Taken together, the benchmark suggests that
influence on research design and on policy discussion is achievable, while
decision-makers' use of findings is harder to show.

## Strengths and limitations

This review has three strengths. All cases were scored on a common framework
with rules fixed before scoring and two independent coders. Failure cases were
included and scored on the same terms as successes. And the review includes
cases from a middle-income country, addressing a gap in the existing evidence
[@todowede2023].

It also has limitations. First, it relies on public documents, so practices
that were not reported could not be scored; the high number of NR scores
reflects this. Second, the cases were selected purposively and are not
representative of citizen science in mental health. Third, the evidence for
some cases rests on organisational reports, project websites or news, which may
present projects favourably or selectively. Fourth, the scoring framework is
new and has not been validated beyond this review. Fifth, the unit of analysis
and definition of a citizen required judgement, particularly for failure cases
in which people whose data were used had no research role. Finally, the lead
author founded a company that develops a research platform evaluated later in
this series; the steps taken to limit bias are described in the Methods and
Declarations. We found no Indonesian citizen science project focused on mental
health, which may reflect a true absence or limits of our search.
